speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister Edwin Tong had explained that when Income proposed the transaction with Allianz, it was to find a strong partner that can complement NE in strengthening Income, so that Income can sustain its social mission.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The concern is over the terms and structure of this specific transaction, particularly as seen in the context of the preceding corporatisation exercise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government remains supportive of NE's and Income's efforts to find a strong partner, with Allianz or other partners, to strengthen Income's capital base and market position.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Income is now a corporate entity, it is no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the Registrar of Co-operative Societies, or co-ops for short.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The deal is still subject to MAS' approval under the Insurance Act for Allianz to become a substantial or controlling shareholder.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under the Insurance Act, sections 26 and 27 require a person to seek the prior written approval of MAS to obtain effective control or become a substantial shareholder of a licensed insurer incorporated in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When assessing an application under section 26 or 27, MAS considers a range of criteria on prudential grounds, such as the financial strength and track record of the applicant, and whether it is fit and proper.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This assessment is focused primarily on the suitability of the proposed substantial shareholder or person obtaining effective control.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Minister-in-charge of MAS will also take into account prudential considerations under the Insurance Act in making his decision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Bill applies specifically to a licensed insurer that is the subject of an application under section 26 or 27 of the Insurance Act, where: (a) the licensed insurer is a co-op; (b) the licensed insurer has acquired the principal business or undertaking of a co-op; or (c) a co-op is a substantial shareholder or has effective control of the licensed insurer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The second and third limbs will apply to Income as it took on the assets of Income co-op when the latter corporatised, and NE, as a co-op, is currently Income's majority shareholder.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Bill will allow the Minister-in-charge of MAS to impose conditions to an approval involving such applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also provides that there will be no avenue for appeals to the Minister in respect of MAS' decision not to approve an application on the basis that the Minister has withheld approval.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are making the amendments on an urgent basis because the proposed transaction is under active consideration by Income's shareholders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among my concerns then were whether with NE ceding majority control of Income, would Income still be able to do the social good, as what they have done before all these years, which is to provide affordable essential insurance products, particularly to the underserved.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I also asked if there is social value in NE retaining control of Income Insurance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In his reply, Minister of State Alvin Tan shared that the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and Income has given assurance to keep the premiums affordable for Income's low-cost schemes for its members and that they reiterated its commitment to its social mission, post-acquisition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan also mentioned that Allianz has represented that it would honour Income's existing policies, participate in the national insurance programmes and continue its charity commitments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the same session in August, in the replies to related questions on behalf of MAS, Minister Chee Hong Tat also shared with the House then that MAS is still in the midst of assessing the application.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: He said that MAS would consider a range of criteria in assessing the deal, such as its track record, fitness, reputation, propriety, including the financial capacity of the proposed shareholder to support the insurer when needed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But I must admit that, in my heart, I thought it is a done deal in due course.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, it came as a surprise to hear the Ministerial Statement by Minister Edwin Tong on Monday that the deal would be blocked on grounds of public interest.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: MCCY has allowed this exemption then on the basis that Income will continue with its social mission and as a company it would build up its capital resources and enhance its financial strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, this capital extraction exercise of S$1.85 billion appears to run counter to the basis in which the Ministerial exemption was granted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Clearly, with the cash extraction, the capital position of the new entity would not be accretive and hence, also put into question how the company can continue to fulfil its social mission.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Social co-operatives and the not-for-profit enterprises play an indispensable role to help keep essential products and services affordable and accessible; and also, importantly, plug the gaps for those areas not covered by commercial enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Singapore's context, entities that are run as social co-operatives, such as those like NTUC, have always been a useful instrument for the Government to do some of the public good, such as helping to stabilise inflation, to manage cost of living, to provide more affordable, inclusive products, whether it is healthcare, eldercare, childcare, groceries or insurance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I remembered during the early days of COVID-19, NTUC Fairprice and its pharmacy arm, Unity, were at the forefront of managing the distribution of masks and sanitisers and also helping to keep prices steady and to curb profiteering.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Social co-operatives do help to strengthen our social and economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the case of corporatised insurance, where it enjoys the exemption of section 88 of the CSA, I would argue that the Government should requires NE to remain as the majority shareholder of Income for a prescribed number of years so that it can continue to steward Income to carry out its social mission.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They may have made undertakings, but it is important to have the majority control.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I also hope that the Government and the NTUC can align and reaffirm its social missions of with regard to co-operatives and refresh an updated roadmap on the roles of our major social co-operatives in our economy and our society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore has always been an attractive destination for foreign direct investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Inward investments have helped to build our economic capabilities, brings in the needed capital to fuel growth, create good paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our openness to foreign investments is one of our key success factors for our economic progress and it brings in exciting opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, my other concerns would be whether the rejection of the Allianz transaction on grounds of public interest would have any impact on our reputation as a global centre that welcome international investments, which is my second ask.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That is, to call on the Government to reaffirm this long-standing policy, to position Singapore as an investment friendly global hub that welcome value adding economic investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The point is, we have never been averse to foreign investors acquiring Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We want to be an appealing global economic hub where as far as possible free market principles prevails.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is the uniqueness of the Singapore model, what we call "same-same but different".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We want to be a vibrant economy but we want to have the social safeguard.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is to borrow the words of Mr Lim Swee Say, the former Secretary-General of NTUC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the deal is bad for Singapore and its public interest, it should be blocked.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I will make two key arguments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I shall begin by documenting a troubling sequence of events in the run-up to the public announcement on the Allianz-Income deal and its aftermath, involving what appears to be multiple sources of information failures within Government, and between the Government and the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Next, I will offer some thoughts on guiding principles for how we may wish to proceed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will explain why this is not merely a mild oversight in informational exchange, but a communication breakdown that may reveal some troubling pathologies with how the Government conveys information within itself and with the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, it will be useful to understand just how much MAS knew about Allianz's capital extraction plan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But MAS' oversight functions extend beyond prudential regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Its mandate includes the supervision of domestic systemically important insurers (DSIIs), of which Income Insurance is one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Besides capital requirements, which is of course central to macro prudential supervision, a holistic assessment, risk assessment, would also entail the evaluation of, and I quote, from the MAS' own published framework on risk assessments, "qualitative criteria such as brand value and strategic importance".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Did MAS not believe that a capital extraction plan, contrary to Income's historical mission, would not potentially contribute to elevated post-acquisition risk?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, if there were to be a sudden exit of Income policy-holders resulting from the deal, surely this would give rise to undesirable financial instability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could such a holistic assessment be completed in the brief period between mid-July and the time of the public announcement?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This begs the question of why this link was not made, given how the exemption is in the public records, and surely a S$2 billion surplus would be material to the sort of prudential considerations that MAS concerns itself with in its supervision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Apparently, it was then that MAS recognised that there could be larger considerations beyond just prudential ones and hence, only then did the Government began the process of working together in a whole-of-Government manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if it is only me who finds it troubling that there was no coordinated discussion between the two major relevant regulators, MAS and MCCY, in advance of the proposed deal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Has our civil service become sufficiently siloed in their treatment of what falls under which agency or Ministry's purview that even for transactions of such prominence, no joint working group was convened to ensure sufficient information exchange in advance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could we be assured that this is a one-off occurrence, or is this a canary in a coal mine that is telling us that we need to look more carefully at how well our Government departments exchange relevant data and information?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fourth, in September, I had filed a Parliamentary Question asking if MAS had required a commitment from Allianz to provide a capital adequacy injection to grow Income Insurance Limited across its business lines, beyond the S$2.2 billion that Allianz would pay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the time, I, like many others, were unaware of the proposed capital extraction plan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presumably, however, the Government was, but in the terse response received from Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, it was only suggested that MAS would "assess Income Insurance's business strategy and capital management plan after Allianz submits its application to obtain effective control and be a substantial shareholder of Income".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: No reference was made to the capital extraction plan, yet as shared by the Ministers on Monday, these concerns were already conveyed to MCCY by then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, why was the same information not shared as a response to my Parliamentary Question?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps more important, why was so much of the debate in the House two months ago and the constant refrain by NE itself so fixated on capital injections when in reality, Income was much more likely to be facing capital extraction?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, I am left to conclude that on the assumption that the Government was neither wilfully withholding information from one governmental agency to another, nor to a direct question posed by a Member of Parliament, then at the least, there appears to have been multiple breakdowns of communication between different governmental entities in the exchange of pertinent information over the transaction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the objection to the original deal, it is natural for us to ask what is next.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do not propose to be speculative given how we do not even have the contours of a potential revised deal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But given how NE and Income Insurance have publicly stated that they will work closely with the relevant stakeholders to decide on next steps and how market motivations that led to the original deal indeed remain, it would not be a stretch to imagine that there will be a revised effort to raise capital for Income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What have we learned from public feedback over this episode?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, it is clear that there is strong public sentiment that values the historical social objectives of Income Insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding how Income is already a corporate entity ultimately answerable to its shareholders, the boards of Income Insurance as well as NE do need to be more sensitive to how their stewardship should reflect the concerns of stakeholders as well and to render appropriate consideration to its social mission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The need to be cognisant of social objectives notwithstanding, the minority shareholders of Income, many of whom are aged and have sought liquidity for years, should be allowed to exit with a fair value for their holdings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, future transactions of such importance should, right at the outset, involve the establishment of a multi-Ministry task force with representatives from all the relevant bodies to ensure that the sorts of communication breakdowns that occurred this round do not recur.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is not difficult to see how, depending on the sector, not only MAS and MCCY but also the Ministry of Manpower, Ministry of Digital Development and Information and Ministry of Trade and Industry may be involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Traditionally, such whole-of-Government efforts would be coordinated via the Prime Minister's Office.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may well be called for in future such transactions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The simplistic answer, of course, is simply that income does not fall within the existing gazetted list of designated entities under SIRA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so may open the door to determining whether SIRA-style restrictions or other measures are necessary for future transactions of this nature, thereby ensuring that future transactions are evaluated not purely on a commercial basis but also for their broad alignment with Singapore's interests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will lend further credence to the transparency and predictability of our regulatory approach and will go some way toward restoring our nation's reputation as a reliable institutional partner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the long run, this will benefit both local and foreign stakeholders in our financial sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If this were the reason alone, the WP would have no objection to the Bill, beyond clarifications to the points that I have raised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, the Bill does raise other legal and procedural considerations which I will leave my Sengkang colleague, He Ting Ru, to elaborate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Income-Allianz deal is one which has drawn a high level of public interest.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The majority of Singaporean households have insurance policies with NTUC Income or Income Insurance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the whole-of-Government way of doing things will continue to be a mainstay and strength of the Singapore Civil Service.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I had raised this issue in Parliament two days ago and we had since have more clarity on how the MAS team had been assessing the deal on prudential grounds.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appreciate that MAS shared information, which they assessed to be relevant to MCCY.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I fully support the amendments in the interests of the public, would we be setting a precedent where investors need to factor in potentially unexpected changes to regulations?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On one hand, I am heartened that our Government is open to feedback even as it strives to balance different priorities and competing demands.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, we must uphold Singapore's reputation as an open, transparent and rules-based city which is pro-business and welcomes foreign investments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened that the Government has confirmed that it will be open to new proposals if the concerns are addressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so when it adversely affects the rights and interests of persons and has the potential to hurt Singapore's reputation for certainty, stability and predictability of our commercial laws.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It should not be taken lightly and the WP's position when the Constitution was amended a year ago as a precautionary measure, reflects our general concern over retrospective amendments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this case, while it is true that MAS’ approval of Allianz's proposed acquisition of 51% of Income remains pending, we note that the transaction had previously been signed and announced, albeit conditional upon receiving regulatory approval amongst others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It can thus be seen to be a live transaction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, I believe that there is a risk that the amendments proposed in this Bill, along with their urgent nature, would be seen to be retrospective by players in our corporate finance landscape.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even if some were to argue that this Bill's acts do not fall within the realm of having retrospective effect, there is a second principle of legal and regulatory certainty in the context of Singapore's corporate finance landscape to consider.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This was also alluded to by Members Liang Eng Hwa and Joan Pereira in their speeches.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having worked on a number of highly complex multi-billion-dollar mergers and acquisitions, and structured finance transactions across multiple jurisdictions spanning the globe, I know how invaluable it is to have certainty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In such deals, there are many moving parts and a number of complicated regulatory regimes ranging from takeover codes, listing rules, merger control, catch all laws governing natural and national interests, and also financial rules for lawyers and other financial advisors to consider.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also why it is also standard practice for parties to engage with regulators early on in the preparatory process long before any public announcements are made so that parties can understand potential impediments to their transactions, assess the risk of a regulator blocking the transaction and to address these through their structuring of the transaction, including on occasion giving irrevocable and legally binding undertakings to do or not do certain things for a fixed time period post-completion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is also the case here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is fair that we ask whether the amendments proposed in this Bill, especially under a Certificate of Urgency, which was last used during COVID-19, are in fact strictly necessary to provide the Government through MAS the legal power to block the Allianz’s acquisition of Income.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: MAS' powers are contained in sections 26 and 27 of the Insurance Act 1966.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These sections provide the MAS may approve an application to obtain effective control or become a substantial shareholder of a licensed insurance company if MAS is satisfied that: first, the applicant is a fit and proper person; and second, that having regard to the likely influence of the person, the licensed insurer concerned will or will continue to conduct its business prudently and comply with the provisions of this Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Act also does not say that MAS cannot take into account other factors relevant to its mission, which would include the overall health of Singapore's financial sector as a whole, for example, including the provision of insurance services to the public, and whether the people's interests in having access to affordable and reliable insurance policies and products are served.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, I note that although Income is said to have a social mission, it is also clear that its mission is to provide insurance, which is most definitely a financial service.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, whether Income in whatever form it morphs into in the future conducts its financial services business in a manner that benefits the people of Singapore on the whole, is something that MAS can already take into account in considering whether to give approval under sections 26 and 27 of the existing Insurance Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government can address legitimate concerns raised about how this Bill and its passage may be perceived as harmful retrospective legislation and rushed as legislation, with its attendant negative impact on our reputation as a financial and corporate hub with certainty over laws and regulations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would now like to turn to some questions arising from the proposed Allianz-Income transaction which provided impetus for this Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of the points will be matters that fall within the domain of MCCY, but I believe it is impossible to disentangle MCCY's role in this matter from MAS' role as the approving authority for the transaction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the very purpose of the Bill is to enable MAS to consider the view of the MCCY Minister.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Government therefore clarify four points about this?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the retention of surplus due to legal form change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that Income was not being dissolved but merely changing its legal structure, would this fact alone have been sufficient for MCCY to grant Income's request to keep the surplus?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If the above reason was not sufficient, what specific representations did Income make to MCCY that justified allowing it to retain the surplus?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Did Income detail any new business lines or initiatives it planned to pursue, that would require significant capital thereby justifying the need to keep the surplus?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, the link between surplus and social mission.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Was there an understanding between MCCY and Income that retaining the S$2 billion surplus was tied to Income's commitment to its social mission?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If so, could the Government provide more details on this agreement and how the surplus was intended to support that mission?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Fourth, future restrictions on returning surplus to shareholders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can the Government clarify if its position is that because of the circumstances under which Income was originally allowed to keep the surplus, the company is now restricted indefinitely from returning any part of that surplus to its shareholders?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The philosophical question underlying these four specific questions is, what really is Income's social mission?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During Monday's Ministerial Statement, the MCCY Minister also referred to a lack of assurance that Income would preserve its social mission post completion should Allianz become its majority shareholder.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Government elaborate on this and articulate again what it sees as Income's social mission now and going forward into the future?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, the landscape has changed dramatically since its founding over 50 years ago in 1970.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, would Income's social mission lie in the areas of life insurance policies, or whether other areas such as health insurance may be more important and the focus of a socially-oriented Income?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is important that this issue be viewed looking at the overall big picture.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can point to Allianz's offer document, which mentions that it would continue to honour Income's participation in national-level insurance programmes, continuing its charity commitments, providing low-cost schemes to union members, pledging $100 million over 10 years from 2021 to promote social mobility and support the well-being of seniors, are worthy moves to be sure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, if we leave the question of what is its social mission unanswered, it risks presenting these specific and perhaps narrow matters as central, while missing the wider picture of how Income is fundamentally able to fulfil its social mission as an insurer.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like many Singaporeans of a certain vintage, Income is intertwined with memorable chapters of my life – when my parents first took out insurance savings plans for my sibling and me, when I took on travel insurance for my first trip overseas, and later, when I enrolled my parents and myself in Income’s Shield Plans after I started working.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To my fellow unionists and me, Income, together with the social enterprises under NE’s purview, are consistent partners that our unions and associations have counted on to reinforce NTUC’s social mission of helping workers to earn a better living and live a better life.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I have assisted members who found their lives suddenly upended by severe injury or illness or in some cases, death.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because Income made members’ well-being its focus, I have counted on its insurances to provide much needed financial relief to members who were hit by these life catastrophes and as important, to communicate our care for our members and their families.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Fast-forward to July this year, Income Insurance announced its decision to form a partnership with global insurer, Allianz, to strengthen its finances and financial sustainability to serve the longer-term needs of its customers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Both Income and its holding entity, NE, have been consistent in communicating Income Insurance's steadfast commitment and responsibility towards delivering social good on a lasting basis while charting a durable path to financial sustainability through the proposed partnership with Allianz.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I note the developments which MAS had surfaced when it evaluated the proposed partnership between Income and Allianz, and that these developments had prompted the Government to recommend expanding the MAS’ diligence process to also include consultation with the Minister overseeing co-operatives.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to seek clarification on three areas outlined under section 33A.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, could the Minister advise what is defined as “in the public interest” for the purposes of section 33A?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, what type of conditions could the Minister attach to the approval and what are the considerations guiding how these conditions are determined?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, under what circumstances would the Minister make changes to the conditions and on the same basis, under what circumstances could the licensed insurer apply for a review of the conditions?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because insurance is most valuable when we are most vulnerable, I can appreciate and understand why the Government is seeking to apply both prudential and social perspectives to its evaluation of the proposed partnership between Income and Allianz.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The uncertainties felt by our unionists brought about by the halting of the deal are also understandable.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: My fellow unionists and I do understand and appreciate the reasons why the deal cannot proceed in its current form, as articulated by the Minister of MCCY.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Income must find new ways to navigate the Bill, alongside existential challenges such as insuring an ageing base and expanding cover to include more complex and varied health conditions.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, charity begins at home.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It remains a fact that Income must do well in business to be in the position to do social good.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill thus places the ball back in Income’s court, to consider the implications of the Bill in respect of Income's plans to chart a durable path to long-term financial viability.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In summary, the Bill presents an opportunity for Income and Allianz to articulate how the proposed partnership can do well and do good.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing well translates to safeguarding the best interests of stakeholders, including policy-holders and shareholders, while doing good is about creating an impact footprint that is purposeful, meaningful and lasting in outcomes for workers and the social good.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP had not been in favour of this deal.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In July, Dr Tan Cheng Bock had written on his Facebook page asking for the reasons for breaking a promise.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And in a Facebook post after the 6 August Sitting, my colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, had expressed his hope that the deal would be restructured.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we support the decision to stop this deal, we have concerns about the act of amending the Insurance Act in a hurry in order to block it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This provides confidence to investors, here and abroad, that our regulatory framework is stable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though the Bill we are debating today is tightly scoped, the fact that we are amending the law today so that a specific pending acquisition application can be blocked may be unsettling to investors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under existing law, sections 26 and 27 of the Insurance Act 1966 require the approval of MAS for any application to obtain effective control or become a substantial shareholder of a licensed insurer.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some conditions were listed under which MAS may grant approval.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the words used in sections 26 and 27 is “may approve” and not “shall approve”, it appears to us MAS already has the discretion not to approve the application.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 14 October, during clarification time after the Ministerial Statement on this issue, Members were assured that we would have time for further debate on the sale of Income Insurance during the Second Reading of the Insurance (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I had during that session raised the point that communications on the reasons for the sale of Income Insurance to Allianz had been misleading.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Edwin Tong disagreed and said there was no misleading.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a joint statement from NE and Income Insurance dated 4 August 2024 to explain the need for the sale of Income Insurance, paragraphs 7 and 8 of the executive summary stated that, “In terms of NTUC Enterprise upholding Income Insurance’s social mission, capital resilience is necessary to provide affordable, inclusive insurance on a sustained basis...The circumstances between when Income Insurance was founded and today are vastly different.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the goal of providing affordable insurance remains, the competitive landscape has changed with more than 40 global, regional and local insurers vying for growth in a mature Singapore insurance market.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This also makes strong and continuous capital resilience a pre-requisite for growth, which a social enterprise model alone cannot shoulder.” Does this not create the perception that the sale is necessary due to the need of Income Insurance for more capital?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we reconcile this statement with the fact that by the time this statement was issued on 4 August, an application had already been made to MAS in July to reduce capital by S$1.85 billion and distribute this amount to the shareholders?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would not this capital reduction reduce capital resilience?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the Parliamentary Sitting on 6 August 2024, Minister of State Alvin Tan while answering Parliamentary Questions on this deal repeated the need for capital a few times.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He said: “NTUC has explained the reasons for the deal with Allianz.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current situation for Income cannot be sustained and Income's capital buffers have repeatedly come under pressure.” In response to Mr Liang Eng Hwa’s supplementary question, he again said: “I think if we take a step back, the reasons why Income has gone into this proposed deal is well laid out.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are realities on the ground – competitive, Government stepping in to provide that social assurance, as well as the capital requirements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The capital buffers, for example, were under pressure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, that is the first principle.” In response to Mr Leong Mun Wai’s supplementary question, he said: “Time is the best judge, but let me again put it out very clearly, that number one, Income’s capital buffers have been under pressure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no doubt about this.” He also said: “Then, it also begs the question, could Income and NTUC Enterprise then have looked for other funding sources, which is the question on the ground.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MAS has assessed that even after this huge capital reduction, it is still meeting capital adequacy requirements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this not show that the public and the Government have been misled?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If Minister Edwin Tong still feels that there has been no misleading, I think we will have to agree to disagree and let the public form their own opinion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, however, the Government agrees that the communications have been misleading, I hope it will send a message that this is not acceptable by holding those responsible to account.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This episode has thrown up another issue of concern.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ties between NTUC and the PAP Government are very strong.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, many Secretary-Generals of NTUC are concurrently Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan himself said so on 6 August, "many of us here are advisors to NTUC unions, we have worked very closely with them.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I work very closely with my unions, Singapore Industrial and Services Employees' Union (SISEU).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I work very closely with the co-ops under SNCF.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I meet them very regularly." This close relationship is a double-edged sword.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there are circumstances when this is an advantage, I believe this episode has reminded us to be careful lest the close relationship affect the Government in its regulatory role.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right from the beginning, PSP has not been in favour of this deal.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we also have some reservations about amedning the Bill in a hurry in order to block the deal, because this sets an unsettling precedent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that the Government should, as much as possible, use the existing provisions and laws to assess whether or not a transaction can be approved.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only then can both investors from Singapore and abroad have confidence in the stability of our regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It cast doubts on whether Income, after being acquired by Allianz, could fulfil its social mission.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is important to note that this deal is still only proposed.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The events of the last few months have brought to light a few important issues, with the most important one being how we deal with our national treasures such as Income Insurance.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, control of such carefully nurtured national treasures should never be passed on to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The majority of the Board as well as the seat of the Chairman should always be in control of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While such a strong view coming from someone like me who has spent over 30 years in international finance, where cross-border mergers are commonplace may surprise a few, my view is based on what I believe, that national treasures should be treated as what they are – national treasures – companies that, for generations to come, will provide world-class products and services to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: To be clear, I do not advocate such a Singapore First policy for companies that do not have a social mission to fulfil nor are they considered national treasures.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: My years in international finance have also taught me that the minor criticism we may face in the short term for a strong Singapore First policy will dissipate away quickly.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Nor will such a strong, clear policy discourage foreign capital from buying controlling stakes in our companies that do not have a social mission to fulfil.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Many countries have allowed control of their national treasures to be sold to foreigners now regret it today.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Just ask the many citizens and residents of New Zealand, where all the major banks are controlled by foreigners.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As I had mentioned during the debate in January this year on the Significant Investments Review Bill, perhaps the time has come for us to have a comprehensive all sector approach to review all large foreign investments in entities significant to the daily lives of most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Such a comprehensive all sector approach will make sure no important large deal slips through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With the unique brand that it has, I fail to understand how Income Insurance does not have a larger market share and greater pricing power in our domestic market.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Why has Income’s relevance in the insurance market just decrease over the years?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: That leads me to agree with the view expressed by many that Income Insurance clearly requires strengthening.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: But, in my view, such a strengthening exercise does not mean ceding control to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps what is needed is a new Singaporean controlled Board of Directors with real talent, real experience and a real vision to come up with a coherent seven-year business plan to make Income Insurance a world-class company, operating profitably not only in Singapore but also in other countries in Asia, ex-Japan.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There are plenty of providers of growth equity capital focused on the insurance business that would be willing to take a minority stake in Income Insurance if a coherent, realistic five-year business plan for growth and development would be presented to them.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We have accomplished that in other sectors and I see no reason why we cannot accomplish the same for our insurance business.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This new Board should be given the complete authority as well as full responsibility for recruiting experienced talent from international insurers, who can help develop the right products and services and execute this five- to seven-year business plan that, while protecting Singaporeans first, can also develop a world-class insurance company headquartered in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While I have shared my views on what I consider is the best strategy for Income Insurance, I would like to seek clarifications from the Minister on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One, what kind of a deal with a new investor would satisfy the Government?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Two, what guardrails would be established to ensure that Income will continue to meet its obligations to society?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Three, how can we ensure that any future financial partner can contribute to the financial strength of Income while still preserving its social mission?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Four, how can we ensure that any new financial investor in Income does not make a quick buck by selling out their stake in a very short period of time or taking a large dividend payment?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I also commend the Government, especially the Second Minister of Finance Chee Hong Tat for his strong leadership and moving quickly to bring this Bill for a vote to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill will allow MAS to facilitate the right discussions while maintaining the highest standards of governance.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While we must remain an attractive and competitive market to attract global capital, we must do everything possible to protect the long-term interests of Singaporeans by continuing to careful nurture national treasures such as Income Insurance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As my colleague Ms Hazel Poa has said PSP will support the Bill if it is necessary to block the Allianz-Income deal.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the sake of Singapore and the 1.7 million policy-holders of Income, it is important that we stop this deal in its current form.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After we discussed the deal in this House on 6 August, I expressed my hope that this deal will be restructured so that NE remains as the majority shareholder.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am personally very glad that the Government has listened to the concerns expressed by Mr Tommy Koh, the two former CEOs of Income, Mr Tan Suee Chieh and Mr Tan Kin Lian, and many Income policy-holders, and decided to block the deal.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am seriously concerned at the process by which we arrived at the conclusion to block the deal.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We learned on Monday that MCCY had no prior knowledge of Allianz's offer for Income before it was publicly announced in July.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, it was only after the 6 August Parliamentary Sitting that MAS shared the terms of the proposed transaction and Income's capital reduction plan with MCCY.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I accept that sometimes, because of market sensitive information, it may not be possible to publicly disclose the full details of a proposed transaction.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in this case, we are talking about information being shared within the Government, between agencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All the agencies knew that this issue would be debated in August, because they received notice of our Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is this information that is highly relevant to the proposed transaction being gatekept at different agencies within the Government?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Throughout this whole affair, it seems that every gatekeeper is concerned only about the part of the process owned by them and no one is keeping an eye on the overall outcome.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our system, the buck stops with Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On a major financial transaction involving a national icon like Income that requires regulatory approval, it is Cabinet that must make a final decision.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why does it seem like there was no coordination within Cabinet on the exchange of important information relevant to the transaction before the August Sitting, so that the Government can take a more informed view and we could have had a more productive discussion in August?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On Monday, Minister Chee Hong Tat said that at the time, MAS was still doing technical assessments and did not surface the details of the transaction to the MAS Board before the 6 August Parliamentary Sitting.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Minister Chee Hong Tat and Minister of State Alvin Tan are both members of the MAS Board and would have been in a position to proactively question MAS officials for the full details of the transaction, which would have included the capital reduction plan before they answered questions in this House on 6 August.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 6 August, the officeholders rehashed again and again how Income's capital buffers have come under pressure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, were all these discussions on Income's social mission and capital buffers on 6 August meaningful?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Had the deal gone through, NE would have relinquished control over Income while unlocking hundreds of millions of dollars from the capital reduction exercise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my view, this would have been another sad case of Singapore losing control over a key strategic company for cash, instead of maintaining these companies for our economic development and security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the Global Financial Crisis, capital adequacy standards have been increased significantly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was ever surprised to hear Minister Chee Hong Tat disclosed on Monday that based on the plans submitted, MAS did not have reason for concern as Income was projected to continue to meet regulatory capital requirements with a healthy margin even with a capital reduction.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we trust that MAS officers are highly professional and have conducted a thorough review of the deal from a prudential point of view, can the Minister further explain why MAS does not have any further prudential concerns over the capital reduction plan, especially considering NE's history of having to inject capital into Income over the years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NE and Income Insurance need to come out to explain why they agreed to a capital reduction plan when both parties had in their joint statements on 4 August 2024 stated explicitly that capital resilience is necessary to provide affordable, inclusive insurance on a sustained basis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Explanations are also needed from NTUC Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng for the joint statement he made with the President of NTUC on 5 August 2024 which said, "The NTUC Central Committee was briefed, and after full and serious consideration, the NTUC Central Committee decided to support NTUC Enterprise's consideration of the offer from Allianz".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, when the NTUC Central Committee was briefed on the offer, were they briefed on the full details of the transaction, including the capital reduction plan?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if so, did the NTUC leaders believe in good faith that the offer would enable NTUC and Income to fulfil its social mission from a stronger position?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what were the reasons that led them to reach such a different conclusion from MCCY?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the NTUC Central Committee did not know the full details, then why did NE and Income not brief them on the full details of the transaction?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The leaders of NTUC, NE and Income owe the public a more substantial explanation to this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If yes, I would like to ask what was Allianz's response?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did Allianz offer to withdraw the current deal so that today we do not have to go through this debate?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can do more to improve whole-of-Government coordination when making major decisions that impact areas governed by multiple agencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The debate over the Income-Allianz deal this week has reminded me of another instance during this term of Government when we had to debate a Bill on the Certificate of Urgency in 2021 to restrict the use of TraceTogether and SafeEntry data to only serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In June 2020, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan had assured the public that TraceTogether data will be used only for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, in January 2021, another agency, the Ministry of Home Affairs revealed something different, that the police could access TraceTogether data under the Criminal Procedural Code.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then as it is now, the public has been left with the impression that our government agencies are siloed and coordination within the Government is poor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We cannot fall into the trap of minding the process and missing out the outcome.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, PSP is raising all these questions with only one objective and that is so that we can ensure that our institutions and processes are always aligned and working well to protect the interests of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fortunately, there is a silver lining in this whole saga.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has highlighted the important role played by Singaporeans in checking the decisions of our public institutions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, we saw Singaporeans with expertise and social repute speaking out and helping the public understand complex issues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has helped Parliamentarians, like myself, to voice out more effectively for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While I support the intent behind safeguarding public interest, this raises important questions about the broader regulatory framework we are fostering.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must strike a careful balance between necessary Government intervention and maintaining business transparency, ensuring that regulations do not unintentionally hinder legitimate business activities or innovation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This includes the details of a potential future capital optimisation by Allianz submitted by them to MAS and was consequently met with intervention, which has created significant uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are watching closely to see how this Bill and similar regulatory actions will impact their ability to operate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, transparency forms the foundation of trust between businesses and regulators.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If businesses comply with full transparency, yet still face intervention, what incentive is there for them to continue being transparent in future dealings, especially disclosure or future projection, plans that may or may not come to fruition.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Will businesses feel secure enough to openly share their plans, especially those involving sensitive or confidential decisions?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the ambiguity of this Bill surrounding the term "public interest".

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While it is the Government's prerogative to define public interest and ensure the protection of society, it is important to clarify upfront what specifically constitutes public interest in transactions of this nature.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without a clear definition, businesses face uncertainty about what actions may trigger intervention, which introduces commercial risks into the regulatory process.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, while MAS oversees insurers from a financial perspective, ensuring they are prudently managed on a capital footing, it does not regulate their social mission.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In practical terms, insurers can focus on financial solvency while customer welfare may not always be prioritised, so long as financial regulations are not breached.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: There remains uncertainty around the Government's expectations regarding Income's social mission.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This raises a key question: how far does the Government expect these social obligations to extend?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without clear markers, it becomes difficult for any organisation to construct a deal that aligns with both financial and social responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When these boundaries are not well-defined, businesses face unpredictability, complicating long-term planning and strategic decision-making.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore essential that we continue building on our commitment to transparency, and the trust between businesses and regulators that have allowed Singapore to remain a competitive global hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, establishing clear markers at the outset of any major transaction is essential, especially when significant public interest is involved.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Defining these boundaries from the start allows businesses and regulators to engage with a shared understanding, minimising the risk of misinterpretation, delays, or wasted resources.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For businesses, the last thing they want is to dedicate months, or even years, of resources only to find out late in the process that their plans do not meet regulatory expectations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For regulators, addressing concerns earlier in the process would make interventions smoother, less contentious and more transparent.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Early clarity ensures that both sides can operate efficiently, reducing friction and improving overall outcomes for all stakeholders involved.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the Ministerial Statement also highlighted a delay in MCCY's involvement.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, earlier involvement of relevant agencies could have flagged potential deal breakers sooner, enabling businesses to address concerns early and avoid public intervention.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, I recommend that businesses be given an opportunity to address and correct draft plans before final decisions or interventions are made.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, had Income and Allianz been given the opportunity to address the Government's concerns earlier, before public announcements or interventions, many of the uncertainties and tensions may have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Providing this opportunity would ensure that businesses and regulators work together more constructively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If businesses are not given a chance to resolve issues privately, it may lead to perceptions of unfair treatment or unpredictability, which could affect investors' confidence.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This uncertainty could deter future suitors or investors and affect our global standing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Government must retain the power to act in the public interest, when necessary, particularly those that will affect the lower-income segments of society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must ensure that this power is exercised fairly and predictably, with transparency on both sides.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With even more oversight in future, we need a regulatory environment where businesses understand their obligations with clarity and where the Government can protect public interest without being seen as overreaching.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This balance is critical to maintain trust between businesses and regulators.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we must be cautious about the signals we send to the business community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I support this Bill on the basis that it serves the larger public interest of protecting Income's social mission.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my support, I have three brief clarifications that I hope the Minister will be able to address.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: When Income and Allianz BV entered into this deal, the present law that we are debating today was not in existence.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The deal might well have been structured differently if it were.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And so, my first question is this, how would the Government propose to mitigate the impact of such conclusions being drawn by investors and businesses, both in Singapore and outside Singapore?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My second question is on the history of corporate deals being overturned or blocked by the Government and the enactment of legislation contemporaneously to effect this.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Has this happened in the past, and if so, what are these instances?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Are there any defining factors that the Government can share with us, on when the "public interest" is deemed to be significant enough for interventions like this?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I think more detailed explanations here will go some way towards assuring businesses and the general public, that this is not something that Singapore does regularly or on a whim.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My third question has to do with the applications of sections 26 and 27 of the Insurance Act.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Chee Hong Tat explained on Monday, and earlier today as well, that on an application of sections 26 and 27 of the Insurance Act, MAS had reviewed the high-level submitted information from Allianz based on prudential grounds.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This involved focusing on whether Allianz was fit and proper, looking at its financial strength and track record, and looking at the interests of Income's policy-holders to ensure that these would be safeguarded with a new, strong, substantial shareholder.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The requirement in sections 26(2)(b) and 27(3)(b) of the Insurance Act is that a licensed insurer should continue to "conduct its business prudently", and that MAS' approval may be given if the Authority is satisfied that conditions are met.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I note the Minister's view that there is no explicit provision in the Insurance Act for MAS to consider non-prudential-related factors in assessing such applications.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Just based on the literal wording of the Act though, MAS' approval is not automatic even if the conditions in sections 26(2) and 27(3) are met.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I wonder if it could also have been possible to take a more expansive view of the word "prudent", given Income's activities as a co-operative which provides financial services to the underserved and given the special circumstances behind its journey to corporatisation?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I believe a more detailed explanation on the present limitations of the Insurance Act will help us in this House to understand why these new, very specific amendments are being debated today and why they are required on an urgent basis.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Two months ago, at least in the eyes of the public, the proposed transaction at the centre of our debate today was defended quite robustly in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Income's track record and the many assurances from Income and NE were repeatedly referenced, to justify that Income's social mission will continue to be fulfilled, even after a foreign company acquires a majority stake in it.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the absence of written or legally binding provisions, one cannot draw sufficient comfort or be reasonably confident that such assurances can be upheld, especially when the ownership structure becomes markedly different post-acquisition, and I agree.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To MCCY, this proposal materially changes the complexion of this transaction since the original intentions of the deal on the grounds of capital adequacy can no longer be defended.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: And I agree with this judgement as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Minister, were it not for the issue of capital extraction, would the Government still see fit to accept the assurances of Income and NE regarding its social mission in good faith?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Or would the lack of clear, binding provisions or structural protections alone be sufficient grounds to merit the blocking of this deal?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, notwithstanding my clarification above, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I understand the need for regulatory oversights, there are important clarifications I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this power can be necessary, it raises questions about accountability and transparency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What exactly does "public interest" mean in this context?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be clear guidelines to ensure decisions are made transparently and not subject to varying interpretations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that those affected have a clear understanding of the reasoning behind these decisions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Every decision should be transparent, especially when it directly impacts our people.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I seek clarifications about the extent of the Minister's powers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises a critical question: will there be a set of guiding principles for such decisions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans deserve to know that decisions affecting them are made with their best interests in mind, free from undue influence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidelines can provide that assurance and help maintain trust in the decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must consider the implications of this Bill for global insurers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How we wield these powers could send a strong message to international businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this Bill create uncertainty for global insurers looking to enter Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that our regulatory environment remains predictable and welcoming for foreign investments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has built a strong reputation as a pro-business destination.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could this discretionary power be perceived as a barrier, making global insurers hesitant to invest here?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Might it also discourage entities from collaborating with our co-operatives, fearing heightened Ministerial scrutiny?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to find a balance, one that protects our social objectives while preserving Singapore's status as a regional insurance hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What assurances can we provide to international insurers that decisions will be made fairly and transparently?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we want to keep Singapore competitive, we cannot afford to close the door on international insurers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the Bill provides for an appeals process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it be the same Minister who initially rejected the application, or will there be an independent committee?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For the appeal process to be truly fair, it must be impartial.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the same person makes the decision and hears the appeal, how can we be confident that justice will be served?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An independent appeals process would instill greater confidence in those affected by these decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must ensure that our approach is balanced and transparent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, we need clear definitions of what "public interest" is to avoid ambiguity and ensure accountability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, we must establish guiding principles for the Minister's decision-making to ensure consistency and maintain public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, we need to strike the right balance between protecting our social interests and maintaining Singapore's attractiveness to global insurers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This demonstrates a willingness to work within our regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This also underscores a critical point: mutual respect between private companies and the Government is critical for maintaining a healthy business environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It ensures that while we protect the interests of our people, we remain open to constructive dialogue with global investors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that this Bill positions us for growth while safeguarding the interests of all stakeholders, both local and international.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us keep the process clear, fair and consistent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about protecting our reputation as a trusted financial hub and, most importantly, prioritising the well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us support the amendments with these considerations in mind, so that we can build a stronger, more resilient insurance sector.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has chosen to do the right thing despite it being inconvenient and potentially politically inexpedient.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have closely read Minister Edwin Tong’s Statement and cross-referenced it with Minister Chee Hong Tat's and Minister of State Alvin Tan’s responses to Parliamentary Questions on the deal at the August Sitting.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I set out the relevant facts as the basis for my questions later.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In his August speech, Minister of State Alvin Tan said: “NTUC has explained the reasons for the deal with Allianz.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The current situation for Income cannot be sustained and Income’s capital buffers have repeatedly come under pressure.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC Enterprise has supported Income with capital injections and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But NTUC Enterprise cannot do this on its own.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: That is why Income sought to corporatise in 2022, so that it could consider more options to access more capital”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, as far as Minister of State Alvin Tan and MCCY were aware at that point, the deal would have put in more capital so that Income would be able to continue to fulfil its social mission.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is borne out in Minister Edwin Tong’s Statement.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Edwin Tong said: “MCCY had no prior knowledge of the proposed transaction before the public announcements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When we first saw the announcements, we accepted the intent of the transactions, which is to strengthen Income.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We saw that Income would be engaged in a strategic partnership with a major reputable player in the industry.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would strengthen Income’s capital base and allow it to have more access to capital.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is consistent with the representation that Income had made to MCCY at the point of corporatisation.” The Allianz-Income deal, however, in its filings with MAS, proposed instead to extract capital from Income, by way of reducing share capital and returning it to Income’s shareholders.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: MCCY was alerted to Income and Allianz’s filings by MAS, because MAS had assessed after the August Sitting that it would be relevant to MCCY to look at the proposed reduction of share capital.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The above having been said, I note that in his August speech, Minister of State Alvin Tan had said: “It is still a proposed deal, yet to be approved”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I also note that Minister Chee Hong Tat and Minister of State Alvin Tan were speaking in different capacities and, in fact, on different points.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
