text: Yes, I was going to respond to Ms Hazel Poa's second question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, as I said just now, I am not able to and I am not going to speak on behalf of Income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the Member did make a point and she suggested in her speech that the statement, which I got her to confirm earlier, that capital resiliency following the transaction was misleading.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the point I was trying to make.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Earlier on, we agreed that that is the reference that the Member was making in paragraph 7.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the point really is this, Ms Poa.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The transaction is contemplated between an insurer, Income; and another insurer, Allianz.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also proposed that following the transaction, the plan was to optimise capital.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One of the ways in which it was going to be done was to re-insure a portion or a portfolio of Income's risk.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Taken together, the statement, therefore, that after the transaction is carried out, its capital resiliency would be improved is, in my view, not misleading.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That was the explanation I gave to the Member.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also explained to the Member that we could improve capital resiliency in a number of different ways such that even after capital reduction, we could still have an adequate capital adequacy ratio.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I have two clarifications for the Minister-in-charge of MAS and one clarification for the Minister for MCCY.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: My second clarification relates to the points I made about why the urgency of this Bill, such that within three days, this needs to be passed, going through a Second and Third Reading.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The question here is that the Minister mentioned earlier the reason why we are rushing through this Bill under a Certificate of Urgency is because this deal is under active consideration by shareholders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: From my understanding of this, shareholders can vote however they want, they can consider however they want.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: But honestly, the offer is ultimately subject to regulatory approval and this is why it is called a pre-conditional offer on the offer document.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I am just wondering, I also mentioned in my speech, given that the long-stop date is nine months from the date of announcement, why is there this rush to do this?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: My clarification for the Minister for MCCY is in relation to the exemption granted to the 2023 gazetted Exemption Order.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I believe the Minister mentioned that there is some flexibility needed to allow the use of the surplus to achieve the mission.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just wanted the Minister to clarify that no conditions were imposed on the use of the surplus in that respect.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had answered Ms He's question and when I used the word flexible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was in the context of my answer to Mr Keith Chua's query about the extent to which social mission might evolve.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That was when I used the word flexible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in the context of the exemption, there was a series of discussions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mentioned in my speech on Monday that we engaged with Income over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was on this basis that the corporatisation and the exemption was granted.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The provision that Ms He mentioned, that is inserted more for avoidance of doubt.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We need a Certificate of Urgency because the deal is under consideration by shareholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, to have a long period between the First Reading and the Second Reading before the amended law takes effect, will actually give rise to more uncertainty in the market and for the parties concerned.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why we are putting forth this Bill for Parliament's consideration and for approval.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I see the hands are really hands of Members who have already asked questions.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I will allow there to be a second round of clarifications.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Just to confirm, I see the hands of Ms He Ting Ru, Ms Hazel Poa, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Are there any more clarifications beyond these hon Members?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, I invite the four hon Members to keep their clarifications succinct and clear.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We will start with Ms He Ting Ru, followed by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Mr Leong Mun Wai and then Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I am still a bit confused because, as I mentioned earlier, the deal is a pre-conditional offer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I do not really understand why the Minister is saying that, given that it is under consideration by the shareholders, we have to rush through.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Because shareholders know that regulatory approvals take a certain amount of time and they know that all these are actually being debated and then the amendments are being proposed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I am not entirely sure that the two are necessarily connected.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I accept that Ms He Ting Ru may have a different view, but I have explained why we want to provide greater certainty on the decision and on the changes to the legislation for the different stakeholders, including the shareholders but also other parties who are involved in this deal.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is the reason why we are doing it with a Certificate of Urgency, but, it is, of course, subject to Parliament's approval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I do not plan to prolong this, but Minister Chee Hong Tat had requested that I withdraw an allegation, if I am correct, that there was a communication breakdown between different arms of the Civil Service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I understand I characterised this as a communication breakdown instead, but perhaps Minister Chee Hong Tat is triggered by the word "breakdown".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Again, I am happy to withdraw the statement if he thinks it is a matter of terminology.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He is entitled to use that phrase if he prefers to.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I was referring to his comment that the public officers are unable to share information due to constraints imposed by the government of the day.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That was what I would like to request that Assoc Prof Lim to withdraw, that comment, because that is not true.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do not put barriers to prevent our public service officers to share information.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, in this case, the decision to share information was proposed by the public officers and supported by the political office holders on the MAS Board.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is that he did not quite answer what I have asked in the speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Did the Government or MCCY make an effort to ask Allianz whether there is a way that this deal can be aborted without us having to come and debate a new law and introduce a new law for this?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is maybe one way of doing it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Well, I heard some laughter in the Chamber, but this is very common.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am in the finance industry for a long time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If the regulator comes to you and says, "I think, your deal, maybe you can consider this and that." Then, there will be negotiation going on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that should be something — If you did not do anything on that, then it is okay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am just seeking an answer whether you did ask Allianz for that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is a lot of trust because Income is a company that is under the NTUC and we Singaporeans have a lot of trust in Income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Over the years, because of our support, there is a lot of surpluses built up in terms of the policies, in the policy funds they are accruing to the policy-holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can I ask the Minister whether the Government can do something to remind NTUC that in the future, when they sell the company, if they have a new deal, their social responsibility will also cover their responsibility to the policy-holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is not just the responsibility of the social mission that the Government is talking about.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because it really worries me that you get an acquiror, potentially, and I am not referring to anybody that comes in and what they are interested in is capital restructuring.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When you restructure the capital, you go and find all kinds of surpluses in the company, you know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And another surplus that an insurance company potentially has is in the policy fund of the policy-holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am saying is that I was wondering whether I can get assurance from the Minister that this message will be passed on to NTUC.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I have explained earlier that we have engaged Allianz and what their response is.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not know whether that means he agrees with me that that is not what we should do, or he thinks that that is what we should do.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If he thinks that that is what we should do, then I would say that we have to disagree, because we believe that as the regulator, to uphold the reputation of our regulatory system and the transparency of our financial sector, to be able to continue to attract investors, as what several Members had spoken about, I think it is important that we deal with our licensees in a manner which is above board and that they understand.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you look at the reaction from Allianz, they said they understood the Government's decision and I think that is important because we want to continue to be a place that foreign investors, companies want to come to, create more good jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Mr Leong, I said earlier that it is not for us to tell Income or indeed any party what to do and how to run their business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: You also mentioned that as a policy-holder yourself and you sort of conflated that point with surpluses, and suggested that there might be some risk to the surpluses, these are all subject to capital adequacy ratios that Income is complying with, and in fact, they will be required to comply with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: So, from that perspective, I think you do not have to worry.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I would just like to clarify that my point was not that the capital resilience after the sale is misleading.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If I misunderstood the Minister earlier, I apologise.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: My point has always been that presenting improving capital resilience as the reason for the sale is misleading, because we now see that the capital resilience is improved through re-insurance, not through the sale to Allianz.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: So, that is how I answered her question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: But be that as it may, the point is, in this transaction, they were entering into a transaction with an insurer and had plans to re-insure part of their portfolio of risk.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: And so, the simple point really is, in that context, the statement that was made in the reference the Member gave, paragraph 7, is not misleading, because there will be improvement to capital resiliency after the transaction.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think we have respected the importance of this Bill through a close to four-hour debate.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And I think it is timely to put the question to the House.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The question is, that the Bill be now read a Second time.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: As many as are of that opinion, say "Aye".

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Yes, I listened carefully to Ms He Ting Ru who, if I am not mistaken, said, "We need to register our abstention on this Bill." So, does that apply to just Ms He Ting Ru or all of WP?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Could you stand up, please, so that we can record your abstentions?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: At this point, I wish to state my opinion that the Bill is a Hybrid Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: However, Standing Order 86 provides that notwithstanding the provisions of any Standing Order, when a Certificate of Urgency signed by the President of the Republic of Singapore, has been laid on the table, the Bill to which the Certificate relates, may be proceeded with throughout all its stages until such Bill has been read the Third time.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Standing Order No 86, therefore, takes an urgent Bill outside the ambit of Standing Order No 68.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Bill before the House today can therefore be committed to a Committee of the whole House, despite Standing Order No 68.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Now, Sir, I beg to move that Parliament will immediately resolve itself into a Committee on the Bill.    .
